entries.3dbceb92656287e869deb330488c4855f9135920: <div sID="gen12285" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="101" osisID="Ps.101" sID="Ps.101"/> <div eID="gen12285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12286" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12287" type="x-p"/> David was certainly the penman of this psalm, and it has in it the genuine spirit of the man after God's own heart; it is a solemn vow which he made to God when he took upon him the charge of a family and of the kingdom. Whether it was penned when he entered upon the government, immediately after the death of Saul (as some think), or when he began to reign over all Israel, and brought up the ark to the city of David (as others think), is not material; it is an excellent plan or model for the good government of a court, or the keeping up of virtue and piety, and, by that means, good order, in it: but it is applicable to private families; it is the householder's psalm. It instructs all that are in any sphere of power, whether larger or narrower, to use their power so as to make it a terror to evil-doers, but a praise to those that do well. Here is, I. The general scope of David's vow, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.1-Ps.101.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The particulars of it, that he would detest and discountenance all manner of wickedness (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.3-Ps.101.5">ver. 3-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">8</reference>) and that he would favour and encourage such as were virtuous, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.6">ver. 6</reference>. Some think this may fitly be accommodated to Christ, the Son of David, who governs his church, the city of the Lord, by these rules, and who loves righteousness and hates wickedness. In singing this psalm families, both governors and governed, should teach, and admonish, and engage themselves and one another to walk by the rule of it, that peace may be upon them and God's presence with them.
entries.6d60db28db9128c40897da61399a27cff6781d45: <div eID="gen12287" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12286" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mercy and Judgment; David's Pious Resolution.</title> <div sID="gen12288" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will sing of mercy and judgment: unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , will I sing. <hi type="super">2</hi> I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart. <hi type="super">3</hi> I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; <hi type="italic">it</hi> shall not cleave to me. <hi type="super">4</hi> A froward heart shall depart from me: I will not know a wicked <hi type="italic">person.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath a high look and a proud heart will not I suffer. <hi type="super">6</hi> Mine eyes <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me. <hi type="super">7</hi> He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight. <hi type="super">8</hi> I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12289" type="x-p"/> David here cuts out to himself and others a pattern both of a good magistrate and a good master of a family; and, if these were careful to discharge the duty of their place, it would contribute very much to a universal reformation. Observe, <div eID="gen12289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12290" type="x-p"/> I. The chosen subject of the psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will sing of mercy and judgment,</hi> that is, <div eID="gen12290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12291" type="x-p"/> 1. Of God's mercy and judgment, and then it looks back upon the dispensations of Providence concerning David since he was first anointed to be king, during which time he had met with many a rebuke and much hardship on the one hand, and yet, on the other hand, had had many wonderful deliverances wrought for him and favours bestowed upon him; of these he will sing unto God. Note, (1.) God's providences concerning his people are commonly mixed—<hi type="italic">mercy and judgment;</hi> God has set the one over-against the other, and appointed them April-days, showers and sunshine. It was so with David and his family; when there was mercy in the return of the ark there was judgment in the death of Uzza. (2.) When God in his providence exercises us with a mixture of mercy and judgment it is our duty to sing, and sing unto him, both of the one and of the other; we must be suitably affected with both, and make suitable acknowledgments to God for both. The Chaldee-paraphrase of this is observable: <hi type="italic">If thou bestowest mercy upon me,</hi> or <hi type="italic">If thou bring any judgment upon me, before thee, O Lord! will I sing my hymns for all.</hi> Whatever our outward condition is, whether joyful or sorrowful, still we must give glory to God, and sing praises to him; neither the laughter of a prosperous condition nor the tears of an afflicted condition must put us out of tune for sacred songs. Or, <div eID="gen12291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12292" type="x-p"/> 2. It may be understood of David's mercy and judgment; he would, in this psalm, promise to be merciful, and just, or wise, for judgment is often put for discretion. To do justly and love mercy is the sum of our duty; these he would covenant to make conscience of in that place and relation to which God had called him and this in consideration of the various providences of God that had occurred to him. Family-mercies and family-afflictions are both of them calls to family-religion. David put his vow into a song or psalm, that he might the better keep it in his own mind and frequently repeat it, and that it might the better be communicated to others and preserved in his family, for a pattern to his sons and successors. <div eID="gen12292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12293" type="x-p"/> II. The general resolution David took up to conduct himself carefully and conscientiously in his court, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.2">v. 2</reference>. We have here, <div eID="gen12293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12294" type="x-p"/> 1. A good purpose concerning his conversation—concerning his conversation in general (how he would behave himself in every thing; he would live by rule, and not at large, not walk at all adventures; he would, though a king, by a solemn covenant bind himself to his good behaviour), and concerning his conversation in his family particularly, not only how he would walk when he appeared in public, when he sat in the throne, but how he would <hi type="italic">walk within his house,</hi> where he was more out of the eye of the world, but where he still saw himself under the eye of God. It is not enough to put on our religion when we go abroad and appear before men; but we must govern ourselves by it in our families. Those that are in public stations are not thereby excused from care in governing their families; nay, rather, they are more concerned to set a good example of <hi type="italic">ruling their own houses well,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4">1 Tim. iii. 4</reference>. When David had his hands full of public affairs, yet he returned to bless his house, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">2 Sam. vi. 20</reference>. He resolves, (1.) To act conscientiously and with integrity, to <hi type="italic">walk in a perfect way,</hi> in the way of God's commandments; that is <hi type="italic">a perfect way,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the law of the Lord is perfect.</hi> This he will walk in <hi type="italic">with a perfect heart,</hi> with all sincerity, not dissembling either with God or men. When we make the word of God our rule, and are ruled by it, the glory of God our end, and aim at it, then we walk <hi type="italic">in a perfect way with a perfect heart.</hi> (2.) To act considerately and with discretion: <hi type="italic">I will behave myself wisely; I will understand</hi> or <hi type="italic">instruct myself</hi> in a perfect way, so some. I will walk circumspectly. Note, We must all resolve to walk by the rules of Christian prudence in the ways of Christian piety. We must never turn aside out of the perfect way, under pretence of <hi type="italic">behaving ourselves wisely;</hi> but, while we keep to the good way, we must be <hi type="italic">wise as serpents.</hi> <div eID="gen12294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> 2. A good prayer: <hi type="italic">O when wilt thou come unto me?</hi> Note, It is a desirable thing, when a man has a house of his own, to have God come to him and dwell with him in it; and those may expect God's presence that walk with <hi type="italic">a perfect heart</hi> in <hi type="italic">a perfect way.</hi> If we compare the account which the historian gives of David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14">1 Sam. xviii. 14</reference>), we shall find how exactly it answers his purpose and prayer, and that neither was in vain. David, as he purposed, <hi type="italic">behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and,</hi> as he prayed, <hi type="italic">the Lord was with him.</hi> <div eID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12296" type="x-p"/> III. His particular resolution to practise no evil himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will set no wicked thing before my eyes;</hi> I will not design nor aim at any thing but what is for the glory of God and the public welfare." He will never have it in his eye to enrich himself by impoverishing his subjects, or enlarge his own prerogative by encroaching on their property. In all our worldly business we must see that what we set our eyes upon be right and good and not any forbidden fruit, and that we never seek that which we cannot have without sin. It is the character of a good man that he shuts his eyes from seeing evil, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa. xxxiii. 15</reference>. "Nay, I <hi type="italic">hate the work of those that turn aside</hi> from the paths of equity (<reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job xxxi. 7</reference>), not only I avoid it, but I abhor it; <hi type="italic">it shall not cleave to me.</hi> If any blot of injustice should come on my hands, it shall be washed off quickly." <div eID="gen12296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12297" type="x-p"/> IV. His further resolution not to keep bad servants, nor to employ those about him that were vicious. He will not countenance them, nor show them any favour, lest thereby he should harden them in their wickedness, and encourage others to do like them. He will not converse with them himself, nor admit them into the company of his other servants, lest they should spread the infection of sin in his family. He will not confide in them, nor put them in power under him; for those who hated to be reformed would certainly hinder every thing that is good. When he comes to mention particulars he does not mention drunkards, adulterers, murderers or blasphemers; such gross sinners as these he was in no danger of admitting into his house, nor did he need to covenant particularly against having fellowship with them; but he mentions those whose sins were less scandalous, but no less dangerous, and in reference to whom he needed to stand upon his guard with caution and to behave himself wisely. He will have nothing to do, 1. With spiteful malicious people, who are ill-natured, and will bear a grudge a great while, and care not what mischief they do to those they have a pique against (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">A froward heart</hi> (one that delights to be cross and perverse) <hi type="italic">shall depart from me,</hi> as not fit for society, the bond of which is love. <hi type="italic">I will not know,</hi>" that is, "I will have no acquaintance or conversation, if I can help it, with such <hi type="italic">a wicked person;</hi> for a little of the leaven of malice and wickedness will leaven the whole lump." 2. With slanderers, and those who take a pleasure in wounding their neighbour's reputation secretly (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Whoso privily slanders his neighbour,</hi> either raises or spreads false stories, to the prejudice of his good name, <hi type="italic">him will I cut off</hi> from my family and court." Many endeavour to raise themselves into the favour of princes by unjust representations of persons and things, which they think will please their prince. <hi type="italic">If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Prov. xxix. 12</reference>. But David will not only not hearken to them, but will prevent the preferment of those that hope thus to curry favour with him: he will punish not only him that falsely accuses another in open court, but him that privily slanders another. I wish David had remembered this vow in the case of Mephibosheth and Ziba. 3. With haughty, conceited, ambitious people; none do more mischief in a family, in a court, in a church, for <hi type="italic">only by pride comes contention:</hi> "Therefore him <hi type="italic">that has a high look and a proud heart will I not suffer;</hi> I will have no patience with those that are still grasping at all preferments, for it is certain that they do not aim at doing good, but only at aggrandizing themselves and their families." God resists the proud, and so will David. 4. With false deceitful people, that scruple not to tell lies, or commit frauds (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He that worketh deceit,</hi> though he may insinuate himself into my family, yet, as soon as he is discovered, <hi type="italic">shall not dwell within my house.</hi>" Some great men know how to serve their own purposes by such as are skilful to deceive, and they are fit tools for them to work by; but David will make use of no such persons as agents for him: <hi type="italic">He that tells lies shall not tarry in my sight,</hi> but shall be expelled the house with indignation. Herein David was <hi type="italic">a man after God's own heart,</hi> for a proud look and a lying tongue are things which God hates; and he was also a type of Christ, who will, in the great day, banish from his presence <hi type="italic">all that love and make a lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Rev. xxii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen12297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12298" type="x-p"/> V. His resolution to put those in trust under him that were honest and good (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">My eyes shall be upon the faithful in the land.</hi> In choosing his servants and ministers of state he kept to the land of Israel and would not employ foreigners; none shall be preferred but true-born Israelites, and those such as were Israelites indeed, the <hi type="italic">faithful in the land;</hi> for even in that land there were those that were unfaithful. These faithful ones his eyes shall be upon, to discover them and find them out; for they were modest, did not crowd into the city to court preferment, but lived retired in the land, in the country, out of the way of it. Those are commonly most fit for places of honour and trust that are least fond of them; and therefore wise princes will spy out such in their recesses and privacies, and take them to dwell with them and act under them. <hi type="italic">He that walks in a perfect way,</hi> that makes conscience of what he says and does, <hi type="italic">shall serve me.</hi> The kingdom must be searched for honest men to make courtiers of; and, if any man is better than another, he must be preferred. This was a good resolution of David's; but either he did not keep to it or else his judgment was imposed upon when he made Ahithophel his right hand. It should be the care and endeavour of all masters of families, for their own sakes and their children's, to take such servants into their families as they have reason to hope fear God. The Son of David has his eyes upon <hi type="italic">the faithful in the land;</hi> his secret is with them, and they <hi type="italic">shall dwell with him.</hi> Saul chose servants for their goodliness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.16">1 Sam. viii. 16</reference>), but David for their goodness. <div eID="gen12298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12299" type="x-p"/> VI. His resolution to extend his zeal to the reformation of the city and country, as well as of the court (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will early destroy all the wicked of the land,</hi> all that are discovered and convicted; the law shall have its course against them." He would do his utmost to <hi type="italic">destroy all the wicked,</hi> so that there might be none left that were notoriously wicked. He would do it early; he would lose no time and spare no pains; he would be forward and zealous in promoting the reformation of manners and suppression of vice; and those must rise betimes that will do anything to purpose in the work. That which he aimed at was not only the securing of his own government and the peace of the country, but the honour of God in the purity of his church, <hi type="italic">That I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the Lord.</hi> Not Jerusalem only, but the whole land, was the <hi type="italic">city of the Lord;</hi> so is the gospel-church. It is the interest of the <hi type="italic">city of the Lord</hi> to be purged from <hi type="italic">wicked doers,</hi> who both blemish it and weaken it; and it is therefore the duty of all to do what they can, in their places, towards so good a work, and to be zealously affected in it. The day is coming when the Son of David shall cut off all wicked doers from the new Jerusalem, for there shall not enter into it any that do iniquity.  <chapter eID="Ps.101"/> <div eID="gen12299" type="x-p"/>

entries.6f4fae2dddb9aedcfe7baa3163b60ec74125cc5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6647"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 101</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8">Psa 101:1-8</reference>. In this Psalm the profession of the principles of his domestic and political government testifies, as well as actions in accordance with it, David's appreciation of God's mercy to him, and His judgment on his enemies: and thus he sings or celebrates God's dealings.</title> <div sID="gen10179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6647"/>2. He avows his sincere purpose, by God's aid, to act uprightly (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Ge 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.30">Psa 18:30</reference>). <div eID="gen10179" type="x-p"/>
entries.727d76f38c5c0c736070c0c0209366e25190ed62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6648"/><div sID="gen10180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6648"/><hi type="bold">3. set ... eyes--</hi>as an example to be approved and followed.<div eID="gen10180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no wicked thing--</hi>literally, "word," plan or purpose of Belial (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.8">Psa 41:8</reference>).<div eID="gen10181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work of ... aside--</hi>apostates.<div eID="gen10182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not cleave to me--</hi>I will not be implicated in it (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1-Ps.1.3">Psa 1:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen10183" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c98fe7a1261f9bb132d0fd89872c03041b9338b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6649"/><div sID="gen10184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6649"/><hi type="bold">4. A froward heart--</hi>or, "perverse heart" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Psa 18:26</reference>). Such a temper I will not indulge, nor even know evil or wickedness. <div eID="gen10184" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bf3382ff594479a1c5c5ad363e1355b34a90596: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6650"/><div sID="gen10185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6650"/>5-6. The slanderers and haughty persons, so mischievous in society, I <hi type="bold">will disown; but--</hi><div eID="gen10185" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ba2d58eeab4f6b65c657f8864fbb8c6a6189f95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6652"/><div sID="gen10187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6652"/><hi type="bold">7. not dwell--</hi>literally, "not sit," or tarry, or be established. <div eID="gen10187" type="x-p"/>
entries.98b0f1a2f0af12616413ad1d0fd5816d4254dcb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6653"/><div sID="gen10188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6653"/><hi type="bold">8. will early--</hi>or, "diligently."<div eID="gen10188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">city of the Lord--</hi>or, "holy place" (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>), where wicked men shall not be tolerated. <chapter eID="Ps.101"/>

entries.e1d42ad7246e039b8633f591fc582f501badd96f: <div eID="gen21944" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21945" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21946" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21946" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21945" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21947" type="x-p"/> The subject proposed, mercy and judgment, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.1">Psa 101:1</reference>. The psalmist's resolution in respect to his private conduct, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.2">Psa 101:2</reference>. He will put away evil, inward and outward, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.3">Psa 101:3</reference>. No evil person shall stand in his presence, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.4">Psa 101:4</reference>; nor any slanderer of his neighbor, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.4">Psa 101:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>. He will encourage the faithful and upright, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.6">Psa 101:6</reference>; but the deceitful, the liars, and the profligate, he will cast out of the city of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>. <div eID="gen21947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21948" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew and all the Versions attribute this Psalm to David. It shows us the resolutions he formed when he came to the throne; and it is a perfect model according to which a wise prince should regulate his conduct and his government. <div eID="gen21948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21949" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21950" type="x-p"/> I will sing of mercy and judgment - David might say, Adverse and prosperous providences have been of the utmost use to my soul; therefore, I will thank God for both. Or, as he was probably now called to the government of all the tribes, he might make a resolution that he would show חסד chesed, incessant benevolence, to the upright; and משפט mishpat, the execution of judgment, to the wicked; and would make the conduct of God the model of his own.
entries.a93b236ac05645ec9fffd3352faaa69547a89a4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21951" type="x-p"/> I will behave myself wisely - God's law prescribes a perfect way of life; in this perfect way I have professed to walk, and I must act wisely in order to walk in it. <div eID="gen21951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21952" type="x-p"/> When wilt thou come unto me? - I can neither walk in this way, nor grow wise unto salvation, unless thou come unto me by thy grace and Spirit; for without thee I can do nothing. <div eID="gen21952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21953" type="x-p"/> I will walk within my house - It is easier for most men to walk with a perfect heart in the Church, or even in the world, than in their own families. How many are as meek as lambs among others, when at home they are wasps or tigers! The man who, in the midst of family provocations, maintains a Christian character, being meek, gentle, and long-suffering to his wife, his children, and his servants, has got a perfect heart, and adorns the doctrine of God his Savior in all things. <div eID="gen21953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21954" type="x-p"/> The original is very emphatic; אתהלך ethhallech, "I will set myself to walk," I will make it a determined point thus to walk. I will bear and forbear with children, servants, etc., not speaking rashly, nor giving way to bad tempers. Through various motives a man will behave with propriety and decorum among others; but none of these motives operate in his own house where he feels himself master, and consequently under no restraint.
entries.521b04f7dc1668a9ba64d58cff4084c3f5aebd43: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21955" type="x-p"/> I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes - I will undertake no unjust wars; will enter into no sinful alliances; will not oppress my subjects by excessive taxation, to support extravagance in my court. I will not look favourably on things or words of Belial. What is good for nothing or evil in its operation, what is wicked in its principle, and what would lead me away from righteousness and truth, I will never set before my eyes. <div eID="gen21955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21956" type="x-p"/> Them that turn aside - I shall particularly abominate the conduct of those who apostatize from the true religion, and those who deny its Divine authority, and who live without having their conduct governed by its influence, such shall never he put in a place of political trust or confidence by me.
entries.2b1aab51bd63cff388b676f7cd47907f18a742a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21957" type="x-p"/> A froward heart - Rash and headstrong men shall not be employed by me. <div eID="gen21957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21958" type="x-p"/> I will not know a wicked person - I will give no countenance to sinners of any kind; and whatever is evil shall be an object of my abhorrence.
entries.b00fe2d24e06460be51ac05675523094e52fef3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21959" type="x-p"/> Whoso privily slandereth his neighbor - All flatterers and time-servers, and those who by insinuations and false accusations endeavor to supplant the upright, that they may obtain their offices for themselves or their dependants, will I consider as enemies to the state, I will abominate, and expel them from my court. <div eID="gen21959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21960" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee gives a remarkable meaning to the Hebrew, מלשני בסתר רעהו melasheni bassether reehu, which we translate, Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, and which it renders thus, דמשתעי לישן תליתי על חבריה demishtaey lishan telitai al chabreyah: "He who speaks with the triple tongue against his neighbor." That is, the tongue by which he slays three persons, viz., <div eID="gen21960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21961" type="x-p"/> 1. The man whom he slanders; <div eID="gen21961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21962" type="x-p"/> 2. Him to whom he communicates the slander; and, <div eID="gen21962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21963" type="x-p"/> 3. Himself, the slanderer. <div eID="gen21963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21964" type="x-p"/> Every slanderer has his triple tongue, and by every slander inflicts those three deadly wounds. Such a person deserves to be cut off. On this subject St. Jerome speaks nearly in the same way: Ille qui detrahit, et se, et illum qui audit, demergit; "He who slanders ruins both himself and him who hears him;" he might have added, and him who is slandered, for this is often the case; the innocent are ruined by detraction. <div eID="gen21964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21965" type="x-p"/> A high look and a proud heart - One who is seeking preferment; who sticks at nothing to gain it; and one who behaves himself haughtily and insolently in his office. <div eID="gen21965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21966" type="x-p"/> Will not I suffer - לא אוכל lo uchal, I cannot away with. These persons especially will I drive from my presence, and from all state employments.
entries.37b1c242421725b4de271ab60bc3ebab4ce50cc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21967" type="x-p"/> Mine eyes - My approbation. <div eID="gen21967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21968" type="x-p"/> Upon the faithful - The humble, upright followers of God. <div eID="gen21968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21969" type="x-p"/> That they may dwell with me - Be my confidants and privy counsellors. No irreligious or wicked man, whatever his abilities may be, shall be countenanced or supported by me. I will purify my court from the base, the irreligious, the avaricious, the venal, the profligate, and the wicked. <div eID="gen21969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21970" type="x-p"/> He that walketh in a perfect way - He that is truly religious. <div eID="gen21970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21971" type="x-p"/> He shalt serve me - Shall be my prime minister, and the chief officer in my army, and over my finances.
entries.bbb7d8fb539d9ca857798b523a9068c89f119fb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21972" type="x-p"/> He that worketh deceit - that tenets lies - I will expel from my court all sycophants and flatterers. Tiberius encouraged flatterers; Titus burned some, banished several others, and sold many for slaves.
entries.bb2a482f4e4d4b136360c53308dce10e3895bcf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21973" type="x-p"/> I will early destroy - I will take the first opportunity of destroying all the wicked of the land. I will purify my court, purge Jerusalem, and cleanse the whole land of every abomination and abominable person; so that the city of my God, where holiness alone should dwell, shall indeed become the Holy City; that the state may be made prosperous, and the people happy. Such an administration must have been a good one, where such pious caution was used in choosing all the officers of the state.  <chapter eID="Ps.101"/> <div eID="gen21973" type="x-p"/>

entries.90620efd3519eea26996cee149ece8ac9c7c76c8: <reference osisRef="Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8">Psa 101:1-8</reference> <div eID="gen9975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9976" type="x-p"/> This is the “prince’s Psalm,”<note placement="foot">Eyring, in his <hi type="italic">Vita</hi> of Ernest the Pious Duke of Saxe-Gotha, v. 1601, d. 1675, relates that he sent an unfaithful minister a copy of the 101st Psalm, and that it became a proverb in the country, when an official had done anything wrong: He will certainty soon receive the prince’s Psalm to read.</note> or as it is inscribed in Luther’s version, “David’s mirror of a monarch.” Can there be any more appropriate motto for it than what is said of Jahve’s government in <reference osisRef="Ps.99.4">Psa 99:4</reference>? In respect of this passage of <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1-Ps.99.9">Psa 99:1-9</reference>, to which <reference osisRef="Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5">Psa 100:1-5</reference> is the finale, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8">Psa 101:1-8</reference> seems to be appended as an echo out of the heart of David. The appropriateness of the words לדוד מזמור (the position of the words is as in Psa 24:1-10; 40; 109:1-110:<reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">7</reference>; 139) is corroborated by the form and contents. Probably the great historical work from which the chronicler has taken excerpts furnished the post-exilic collector with a further gleaning of Davidic songs, or at least songs that were ascribed to David. The Psalm before us belongs to the time during which the Ark was in the house of Obed-Edom, where David had left it behind through terror at the misfortune of Uzzah. David said at that time: “<hi type="italic">How shall the Ark of Jahve come to me</hi> (the unholy one)?” 2Sa 6:8. He did not venture to bring the Ark of the Fearful and Holy One within the range of his own house. In our Psalm, however, he gives utterance to his determination as king to give earnest heed to the sanctity of his walk, of his rule, and of his house; and this resolve he brings before Jahve as a vow, to whom, in regard to the rich blessing which the Ark of God diffuses around it (2Sa 6:11.), he longingly sighs: <hi type="italic">“When wilt Thou come to me?!”</hi> This contemporaneous reference has been recognised by Hammond and Venema. From the fact that Jahve comes to David, Jerusalem becomes “the city of Jahve,” <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>; and to defend the holiness of this the city of His habitation in all faithfulness, and with all his might, is the thing to which David here pledges himself. <div eID="gen9976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9977" type="x-p"/> The contents of the first verse refer not merely to the Psalm that follows as an announcement of its theme, but to David’s whole life: graciousness and right, the self-manifestations united ideally and, for the king who governs His people, typically in Jahve, shall be the subject of his song. Jahve, the primal source of graciousness and of right, it shall be, to whom he consecrates his poetic talent, as also his playing upon the harp. חסד is condescension which flows from the principle of free love, and משׁפּט legality which binds itself impartially and uncapriciously to the rule (norm) of that which is right and good. They are two modes of conduct, mutually tempering each other, which God requires of every man (Mic 6:8, cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mat 23:23</reference> : τὴν κρίσιν καὶ τὸν ἔλεον), and more especially of a king. Further, he has resolved to give heed, thoughtfully and with an endeavour to pursue it (השׂכּיל בּ as in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.13">Dan 9:13</reference>), unto the way of that which is perfect, i.e., blameless. What is further said might now be rendered as a relative clause: when Thou comest to me. But not until then?! Hitzig renders it differently: I will take up the lot of the just when it comes to me, i.e., as often as it is brought to my knowledge. But if this had been the meaning, בּדבר would have been said instead of בּדרך (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.16">Exo 18:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.19">Exo 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.12">2Sa 19:12</reference> [11]); for, according to both its parts, the expression דוך תמים is an ethical notion, and is therefore not used in a different sense from that in Psa 101:6. Moreover, the relative use of the interrogative מתי in Hebrew cannot be supported, with the exception, perhaps, of Pro 23:35. Athanasius correctly interprets: ποθῶ σου τὴν παρουσίαν, ὦ δέσποτα, ἱμείρομαί σου τῆς ἐπιφανείας, ἀλλὰ δὸς τὸ ποθούμενον. It is a question of strong yearning: when wilt Thou come to me? is the time near at hand when Thou wilt erect Thy throne near to me? If his longing should be fulfilled, David is resolved to, and will then, behave himself as he further sets forth in the vows he makes. He pledges himself to walk within his house, i.e., his palace, in the innocence or simplicity of his heart (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.72">Psa 78:72</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.7">Pro 20:7</reference>), without allowing himself to be led away from this frame of mind which has become his through grace. He will not set before his eyes, viz., as a proposition or purpose (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">Deu 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.10.10">Exo 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.10">1Sa 29:10</reference>, lxx), any morally worthless or vile matter whatsoever (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.8">Psa 41:8</reference>, cf. concerning בליּעל, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference>). The commission of excesses he hates: עשׂה is <hi type="italic">infin. constr.</hi> instead of עשׂות as in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.28">Gen 31:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.20">Gen 50:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">Pro 21:3</reference>, cf. ראה <reference osisRef="Gen.48.11">Gen 48:11</reference>, שׁתו Pro 31:4. סטים (like שׂטים in Hos 5:2), as the object of עשׂה, has not a personal (Kimchi, Ewald) signification (cf. on the other hand <reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Psa 40:5</reference>), but material signification: (<hi type="italic">facta</hi>)<hi type="italic">declinantia</hi> (like זדים, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Psa 19:13</reference>, <hi type="italic">insolentia</hi>; הבלים, Zec 11:7, <hi type="italic">vincientia</hi>); all temptations and incitements of this sort he shakes off from himself, so that nothing of the kind cleaves to him. The confessions in <reference osisRef="Ps.101.4">Psa 101:4</reference> refer to his own inward nature: לב עקּשׁ (not עקּשׁ־לב, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.20">Pro 17:20</reference>), a false heart that is not faithful in its intentions either to God or to men, shall remain far from him; wickedness (רע as in <reference osisRef="Ps.36.5">Psa 36:5</reference>) he does not wish to know, i.e., does not wish to foster and nurture within him. Whoso secretly slanders his neighbour, him will he destroy; it will therefore be so little possible for any to curry favour with him by uncharitable perfidious tale-bearing, of the wiliness of which David himself had had abundant experience in his relation to Saul, that it will rather call forth his anger upon him (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.10">Pro 30:10</reference>). Instead of the regularly pointed מלושׁני the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> reads מלשׁני, <hi type="italic">melŏshnı̂</hi>, a <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> (לשׁן <hi type="italic">linguâ petere</hi>, like עין <hi type="italic">oculo petere</hi>, elsewhere הלשׁין, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.10">Pro 30:10</reference>) with <hi type="italic">ŏ</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ō</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.4">Psa 62:4</reference>) and with <hi type="italic">Chirek compaginis</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>). The “lofty of eyes,” i.e., supercilious, haughty, and the “broad of heart,” i.e., boastful, puffed up, self-conceited (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.25">Pro 28:25</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Psa 21:4</reference>), him he cannot endure (אוּכל, properly <hi type="italic">fut. Hoph.</hi>, I am incapable of, viz., לשׂאת, which is to be supplied as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>, after <reference osisRef="Prov.30.21">Pro 30:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">Jer 44:22</reference>).<note placement="foot">In both instances the Masora writes אותו (<hi type="italic">plene</hi>), but the Talmud, <hi type="italic">B. Erachin</hi> 15 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, had אתו before it when it says: “Of the slanderer God says: I and he cannot dwell together in the world, I cannot bear it any longer with him (אתּו).”</note> <div eID="gen9977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9978" type="x-p"/> On the other hand, his eyes rest upon the faithful of the land, with the view, viz., of drawing them into his vicinity. Whoso walks in the way of uprightness, he shall serve him (שׁרת, θεραπεύειν, akin to עבד, δουλεύειν). He who practises deceit shall not stay within his house; he who speaks lies shall have no continuance (יכּון is more than equivalent to נכון) before (under) his eyes. Every morning (לבּקרים as in <reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">Psa 73:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.23">Lam 3:23</reference>, and לבקרים, <reference osisRef="Job.7.18">Job 7:18</reference>), when Jahve shall have taken up His abode in Jerusalem, will he destroy all evil-doers (רשׁעי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.119">Psa 119:119</reference>), i.e., incorrigibly wicked ones, wherever he may meet them upon the earth, in order that all workers of evil may be rooted out of the royal city, which is now become the city of Jahve.  <chapter eID="Ps.101"/> <div eID="gen9978" type="x-p"/>

entries.a050b15df26624af9d58937a0f094491389b0830:
PSALM 101
David was not as yet put in possession of the kingdom, but having been already created king by the appointment of God, he prepares himself for exercising the government in the best manner. And he not only stirs up himself to perform faithfully the duties of his kingly office by devoutly meditating on this subject, but also engages by a solemn vow to be God’s faithful servant, in order to induce Him to put him speedily in possession of the kingdom.
Psalm 101:1-5
A Psalm of David.
1. I will sing of mercy and of judgment: unto thee, O Jehovah! will I sing psalms. 2. I will behave myself prudently in a perfect way, till thou comest to me:
“Ou, quand viendras-tu a moy?” — Fr. marg. “Or, when wilt thou come to me?”
I will walk in the integrity of my heart in the midst of thy house. 3. I will not set a wicked thing before my eyes: I hate the work
“Toute oeuvre.” — Fr. “All the work.”
of those who turn aside; it shall not adhere to me. 4. The perverse heart shall depart from me: I will not know evil
“Ou, le mauvais.” — Fr. marg. “Or, the evil man.”
5. Whoso slandereth his neighbor in secret, him will I destroy: the man whose eyes are lofty, and whose heart is wide, I cannot endure.
 
1 I will sing of mercy and of judgment What David here says concerning singing must be understood by the reader as intimating that this psalm contains the substance of his meditations with himself, as to what kind of king he would be whenever he should be put in possession of the sovereign power which had been promised him. To sing therefore of mercy and of judgment, is equivalent to declaring in solemn terms, that he would be a just and an upright king. Augustine understands this as meaning that God is to be praised, whether he punish men with severity, or whether he show himself merciful to them; but this interpretation is too refined. David does not speak of God’s secret judgments, but of the due administration of the kingdom, that he might both by words and deeds fulfill his vocation. When he asserts, Unto thee, O Jehovah! will I sing psalms, he acknowledges that it was by the favor of God that he was appointed to so distinguished and honorable an office; for it would have been an act of presumptuous rashness for him to have thrust himself into it, at the mere impulse of his own mind. He very properly comprehends all princely virtues under these two particulars, mercy and judgment; for as it is the principal duty of a king to yield to every man his own right, so he is also required to possess a considerate love and compassion towards his subjects. Solomon therefore justly says, (Proverbs 16:12) “The throne is established by righteousness.”

entries.baa053df82a0a936d981e69fd7f04f4e4a38f773:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="101" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A Psalm of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm was composed by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> between times of Gods promising the Kingdom to him and his actual and plenary possession of it, as appears both from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. and from the contexture of the Psalm, wherein he speaks not of his pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent practice, but of his purpose for the future, and so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lemnly declares his resolution, and obligeth himself to these things when he shall be in a capacity to put them in Exe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cution.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 I Will sing of mercy and judgment <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either 1. of God towards me; of Gods mercy towards me, and of his just judgments upon mine Enemies. Or 2. of mine towards my people, I will in my Song declare my obligation and full purpose to execute mercy and judgment in my Dominion; which are the two Pillars of Government: of which he speaks in the following Verses. Interpreters are much divided which to chuse. Possibly both may be joined together, and the sence may be this, I will praise thee, O Lord, as for all thy other excellencies, so particularly for those two Royal perfections of <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>justice</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>judgment,</ns0:hi> which thou hast so eminently discovered in the Government of the World, and of thy people <ns0:hi>Israel;</ns0:hi> and I will make it my care and business to imitate and follow thee as in other things so especially in those vertues which are so necessary for the discharge of my trust and the good government of thy and my people.</ns0:note>: unto thee, O LORD, will I sing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 I will behave my self wisely in a perfect way <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I will manage all my affairs with wisdom and integrity; which are the two chief qualifications requisite for all men, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 10. 16. and most necessary in Princes.</ns0:note>; O when wilt thou come unto me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">O when wilt thou give me the Kingdom which thou hast promised me, that so I may be capable of executing these good purposes both for my own comfort and for the benefit of thy peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple? Or, without an interrogation, as this Particle is used, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 24. <ns0:hi>when thou shalt come to me,</ns0:hi> to wit, in the perfor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mance of that promise to me. He speaks not exclusively, as if he would not walk wisely and righteously in the mean time, but emphatically, that he would continue to do so when he was advanced to the Kingdom, and that he would not suffer himself to be corrupted by his Royal Power and Dignity, as the Princes of the World commonly were. Withal he may intimate, that now he could not do as he desired, and that by the necessity of his affairs he was forced to make use of such men as he did not like, and to wink at those miscar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riages, which it was not now in his power to reform. God is oft said in Scripture to <ns0:hi>come</ns0:hi> to men when he fulfils a pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise to them, or confers a favour or blessing upon them, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 10. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 20. 24. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 80. 2. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 35. 4. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>! I will walk within my house <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In my own Court and Family, as well as in my publick admini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strations; knowing how great an influence the example of my private conversation will have upon my people either to reform or corrupt them.</ns0:note> with a perfect heart <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This Clause adds weight to the former, I will not onely walk in a perfect or right way (which a man may do for politick reasons or with evil design, but I will do so) with an upright and honest heart, which is most acceptable to God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 I will set no <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thing of Belial.</ns0:note> wicked thing before mine eyes <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, to look upon it with deliberation and design, or with desire and delight, as this phrase here and elsewhere implies. If any ungodly or unjust thing shall be suggested to me, whatsoever specious pretences it may be covered with, as reason of state or worldly advantage, I will cast it out of my mind and thoughts with abhorrency, so far will I be from putting it in Execution.</ns0:note>: I hate the work of them that turn aside <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">From God and from his Laws.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, such work: Or, the Contagion of such Exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples. I will neither imitate nor indure such works, nor such workers.</ns0:note> shall not cleave to me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 A froward heart <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">A man of a corrupt mind and wicked life, such as other Princes chuse and prefer as being suitable to themselves, and to their wicked designs.</ns0:note> shall depart from me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Shall be turned out of my Court, lest they should tempt me or infect the rest of my Family, or be injurious or scandalous to my people.</ns0:note>: I will not know <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Not own nor countenance.</ns0:note> a wicked <ns0:hi>person.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Such as by secret and false informations and accusations of others seek to gain my favour and to advance themselves by the ruine of others; which are the common pests of Courts and Kingdoms;</ns0:note>, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look, and a proud heart <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">These he mentions, because Pride is the common Plague of Courts, and the Fountain of many enormities in Courtiers; it makes them imperi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous and insolent towards the poor oppressed Subjects that re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sort to them for relief; it inclines them to those counsels and courses not which are best for the publick good, but which are most for their own honour and advantage, it makes them oppressive and injurious to others that they may have wherewith to satisfy their own lusts.</ns0:note>, will not I suffer.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Mine eyes <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either 1. to find them out. Or 2. to favour and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage them, as this phrase is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 15. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 39. 12. and 40. 4.</ns0:note> the faithful <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Men of truth, justice and integrity, who will be faithful first to God and then to me and to my people.</ns0:note> of the land, that they may dwell with me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>it</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>abide</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>converse with me,</ns0:hi> in mine House and Counsels and publick administrations.</ns0:note>: he that walketh <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> perfect in the way.</ns0:note> in a perfect way <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">In the way of Gods precepts which are pure and perfect.</ns0:note>, he shall serve me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">In do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mestick and publick employments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:492" />7 He that worketh deceit <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He who shall use any frauds, or cheats, or subtil artifices to abuse or wrong any of my people. Which <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> Cour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiers were more likely to indeavour, because he would not permit any open violence.</ns0:note>, shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He that shall abuse me with lies, as Courtiers usually do their Princes, either to defend and excuse the guilty, or to betray the innocent.</ns0:note>, shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>shall not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> not tarry in my sight <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">I will cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainly and immediately banish him from my presence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 I will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 21. 12.</ns0:note> early <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Speedily and without delay, as soon as I arise in the Morning, or, as soon as I am seated in the Throne, that so I may both prevent all that mischief which otherwise they might do; and hinder the infection of others by their evil example; and discourage and deter all my Subjects from the like practices. Heb. <ns0:hi>In the mornings, i. e.</ns0:hi> every Morning, as the same phrase is used also, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 7. 18. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 73. 14. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 33. 2. The Morning was the time allotted for the exercise of judgment. See <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 21. 12.</ns0:note> destroy all the wicked of the land: that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either 1. from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which, though now in the hands of the Jebusites, he looks upon by an eye of faith as if he had it in possession; which he designed for the chief and Royal City of his Kingdom, and for the seat of the Ark and worship of God. And therefore this place above all others was to be purged and preserved from wickedness and wicked men. Or 2. from the whole Nation or Commonwealth of <ns0:hi>Israel:</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did intend and was obliged to reform not onely that one City, but his whole Kingdom, which also may come under the name of a <ns0:hi>City,</ns0:hi> as being combined and united under one Government: for which reason the name of <ns0:hi>City</ns0:hi> is given both to the whole Church of Christ, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 26. 1. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12. 22. <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 20. 9. and to the great Anti Church, the Kingdom of mystical <ns0:hi>Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bylon, Revel.</ns0:hi> 11. 8, 13. and 17. 18, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
